extracted.intended_audience: readers of Newton's Principia; mathematicians/physicists studying classical mechanics and hydrostatics (Latin original)
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretation and extraction of the propositions, definitions, and corollaries in Book II (De motu corporum in mediis resistentibus & hydrostatica) of Newton's Principia. Focuses on laws for resistance in fluids, spiral motion under varying density and centripetal laws, and hydrostatics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of fluid resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Resistentia corporum sphaericorum in fluidis oritur partim ex tenacitate, partim ex frictione, & partim ex densitate medii. Resistentiae partem illam, quae oritur ex densitate fluidi diximus esse in duplicata ratione velocitatis; pars altera, quae oritur ex tenacitate fluidi, est uniformis, sive ut momentum temporis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that resistance has (at least) three origins: tenacity (giving a uniform/time-proportional resistance), friction, and density-related resistance (proportional to the square of velocity). Notes one may treat uniform resistance arising from tenacity in place of uniform gravitational contribution when analyzing ascent/descent; combinations of uniform and velocity-dependent resistances can be composed as needed (references to earlier propositions xiii & xiv).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma on spiral tangency and limiting right angle (Lemma III)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a spiral PQR cuts all radii SP,SQ,SR in equal angles, draw tangent PT at P; if points P and Q approach and meet, angle PSO becomes right, and the ultimate ratio of rectangle TQ×2PS to PQ^2 (?) tends to a given ratio related to equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric limiting lemma used to relate small-arc/area quantities in spirals as successive points coalesce; used in ensuing theorems to connect instantaneous velocity/area elements and geometric ratios of spiral elements. (Lemma stated and proved with perpendiculars and limiting arguments.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiral motion for density ∝ 1/r with centripetal force ∝ (density)^2 (Propositio XV, Theorema XII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si medii densitas in locis singulis sit reciproce ut distantia locorum a centro immobili, sitque vis centripeta in duplicata ratione densitatis: dico quod corpus gyrari potest in spirali, quae radios omnes a centro illo ductos intersecat in angulo dato.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive proof: by comparing arc decrements from resistance and centripetal action and using the lemma on spirals, Newton shows that for a medium whose density ∝ 1/r and where centripetal force scales as the duplicate ratio of density, a body can travel on a spiral cutting all radii at a fixed angle. The surrounding corollaries give practical formulae linking local velocity, density, and resistance, and indicate how given a spiral one gets proportionality relations between resistance and centripetal force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity equivalence at a point (Corollary to Prop. XV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Velocitas in loco quovis P ea semper est, quacum corpus in medio non resistente eadem vi centripeta gyrari potest in circulo, ad eandem a centro distantiam SP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that the instantaneous speed at a point on the spiral equals the speed that would allow circular motion at that radius in a non-resistant medium under the same centripetal force. Used to relate spiral motion in resisting media to circular-motion benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for spiral vs straight descent (Corollary 4 to Prop. XV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpus gyrari nequit in hac spirali, nisi ubi vis resistentiae minor est quam dimidium vis centripetae. Fiat resistentia aequalis dimidio vis centripetae, & spiralis conveniet cum linea recta PS, inque hac recta corpus descendet ad centrum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a condition comparing resistance and centripetal force (resistance must be < 1/2 centripetal force for spiral motion). If resistance equals half the centripetal force the spiral degenerates into the radial straight line PS and descent to the center occurs accordingly; times scale according to previously derived relations (reference to parabola case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized spiral motion for power-law centripetal force (Propositio XVI, Theorema XIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the medium's density and the centripetal force obey general power laws (centripetal force at P reciprocal to some power of SP), then a body can gyrate in a spiral cutting all radii at a given angle; velocities and densities relate according to those powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeats the preceding method for the case where the centripetal force in P is reciprocal to SP^n (n arbitrary). Deduces that time to describe an element and velocity scale as powers of SP, and hence density at P is reciprocal to a determined power of SP. Corollaries note special cases: if centripetal ∝ SP^3 reciprocal, density/resistance vanish (agreeing with earlier propositions), and if exponent >3, resistance sign may change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and small-body scholium (Scholium after Prop. XVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: These propositions about media with varying density must be understood for very small bodies (so that density differences across the body can be neglected). Assumes resistance proportional to density ceteris paribus; if medium's resistance law differs from proportionality to density, density must be adjusted accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies domain of applicability: analysis pertains to bodies small enough that asymmetric density around the body is negligible. If resistance is not proportional to density, the density field should be modified until the resistance law is matched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse problem: determine centripetal force & medium resistance from a given spiral and velocity law (Propositio XVII, Problema IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire vim centripetam & medii resistentiam, qua corpus in data spirali, data velocitatis lege, revolvi potest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: From the velocity with which the body traverses an infinitesimal arc PQ one gets the time; from the altitude TQ (proportional to centripetal force × time^2) one deduces the centripetal force; from equal-time area elements PSQ and QSR and their difference one finds the body's retardation and thus the resisting force and medium density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct problem: find medium density from given centripetal law and desired spiral (Propositio XVIII, Problema V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data lege vis centripetae, invenire medii densitatem in locis singulis, qua corpus datam spiralem describet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure parallels Prop. XVII: find local velocities from the centripetal law, compute retardation from velocity changes, and deduce density; reference made to earlier explained methods (propositio decima and lemmate secundo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluidum est corpus omne, cujus partes cedunt vi cuiuscunque illatae, & cedendo facile moventur inter se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the working definition used subsequently: a fluid's parts yield to any impressed force and move easily relative to each other. This underlies the subsequent theorems on pressure transmission and equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure in a static homogeneous fluid is equal and transmitted undiminished (Propositio XIX, Theorema XIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluidi homogenei & immoti, quod in vase quocunque immoto clauditur & undique comprimitur, partes omnes (seposita condensationis, gravitatis, & virium omnium centripetarum consideratione) aequaliter premuntur undique, & sine omni motu a pressione illa orto permanent in locis suis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cases demonstrate that (i) no part of a uniformly compressed enclosed fluid will move from its place; (ii) spherical portions are equally pressed everywhere; (iii) mutual contact pressures among parts transmit equality of pressure throughout; (iv) if a fluid in a rigid vessel is unequally pressed it will yield until equality is restored, so a rigid vessel cannot sustain a stronger pressure on one side than the other. Corollary: pressure changes on an external surface cannot change internal motions unless the surface figure changes or relative mobility among fluid parts varies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for submerged bodies and buoyancy (Corollaries to Prop. XIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: A body submerged in a fluid of the same specific gravity neither sinks nor rises nor is forced to change shape by the pressure of the surrounding fluid; if the body's specific gravity exceeds that of the contiguous fluid it will sink, if less it will rise. Thus apparent weight depends on the excess or defect of the body's gravity relative to the fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces distinction between absolute (true) gravity and apparent/comparative gravity (buoyant effect). The excess of true gravity over the fluid's weight gives the 'apparent' weight and determines ascent/descent and the impulse with which the body is driven toward equilibrium (relates to experiments with bodies in air/water).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic paradox: bottom supports weight equal to a cylinder of fluid (Propositio XX, Theorema XV)
rubrics_metrics.description: If spherical, homogeneous fluid is contained in a spherical vessel, the pressure on the bottom sustains the weight of a cylinder whose base equals the bottom's surface and whose height equals the depth of the fluid (i.e., bottom supports the weight of a column of fluid of that base and height).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: decompose fluid into concentric spherical shells; the pressure on each lower surface adds in sequence to give a resultant pressure equal to the summed effect, which equals the weight of a column of fluid of height equal to the total depth. Corollaries: pressure at equal distances from the center is the same regardless of surface orientation; fluids transmit pressure to produce perpendicular rise or flow along cavities/channels without changing the pressure magnitude derived from depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrostatic corollaries on motion and pressure transmission (Corollaries to Prop. XX & XIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluid parts do not acquire motion from the weight of the fluid above except insofar as condensation (compression) or nonuniformity permits; pressure on an immersed body does not change its external shape; if a body is specifically heavier than the surrounding fluid it will sink and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains permanence of shape under uniform pressure (e.g., a submerged rigid body retains form), and that pressure acts through mutual contact producing equilibrium unless condensation or shape changes allow motion; details about transmission through cavities and independence of pressure from orientation of the pressed surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density distribution under centripetal force ∝ 1/r (Propositio XXI, Theorema XVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the density of a fluid is proportional to its compression and the parts are drawn downward by a centripetal force whose magnitudes at places are reciprocally proportional to their distances from the center, then if distances are taken continuously proportional, the densities of the fluid at those distances are also continuously proportional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via slicing into concentric shells, erecting perpendiculars proportional to densities, and showing the density at each location equals the infinite-series sum of pressures from shells above; corollary: given density at two locations one can deduce density at any other via areas associated to a hyperbola construction (practical geometric inversion technique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric-progressive density for geometric progression of radii under inverse-square gravities (Propositio XXII, Theorema XVII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If density is proportional to compression and the parts are drawn downward by gravities reciprocally proportional to the squares of their distances (or other specified power-laws), and the distances are taken in geometric progression, then the densities of the fluid at those distances are in geometric progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses hyperbolic-area arguments and summation of rectangular terms to show that differences of densities correspond to hyperbolic areas; scholium generalizes: for other power laws (gravities decreasing as other powers) corresponding choices of arithmetic/musical or geometric progressions of distances lead to geometric progressions of densities. Also gives a method to compute a density at a chosen altitude from two known densities by area-comparison.
